doc_summary: Lipton and Steinhardt argue that ML scholarship suffers from four trends (speculation presented as explanation, unidentified sources of empirical gains, mathiness, and misuse of language), and propose remedies emphasizing ablations, error analysis, and calibrated claims. The paper stresses that headline results are weak evidence without understanding what drives them.

items.claim: Prefers evidence that isolates what drives a result (ablations, error analysis, robustness checks) over raw headline numbers because a score alone cannot show which factor produced it.
items.quote: We encourage authors to ask “what worked?” and “why?”, rather than just “how well?”. Except in extraordinary cases [39], raw headline numbers provide limited value for scientific progress absent insight into what drives them.

items.claim: Prefers empirical investigations that consider and rule out alternative hypotheses over a single confirming story because untested explanations get repeated as fact.
items.quote: (ii) describe empirical investigations that consider and rule out alternative hypotheses [62];

items.claim: Distrusts benchmark and evaluation setups that look like they test a high-level capability but actually test something shallow, and wants the test validated by probing what it really measures.
items.quote: datasets that appear to test high-level semantic reasoning but actually test low-level syntactic fluency

items.claim: Checks whether a test is easier than it looks by examining what a simple baseline or a single piece of information can already solve, a useful probe for whether an eval setup has exploitable shortcuts.
items.quote: [11] studies a task designed for reading comprehension of news passages and finds that $73\%$ of the questions can be answered by looking at a single sentence, while only $2\%$ require looking at multiple sentences

items.claim: Distrusts claims of human-level capability drawn from artificial, i.i.d. test conditions because they differ from the unpredictable real-world conditions where humans actually operate.
items.quote: The comparison to dermatologists conceals the fact that classifiers and dermatologists perform fundamentally different tasks. Real dermatologists encounter a wide variety of circumstances and must perform their jobs despite unpredictable changes. The machine classifier, however, only achieves low error on i.i.d. test data.

items.claim: Prefers clearly separating speculation from established findings and scoping claims narrowly (e.g., the specific task) over broad suggestive claims because overclaiming misleads readers.
items.quote: In contrast, claims of human-level performance in [29] are better-qualified to refer to the ImageNet classification task (rather than object recognition more broadly).

items.claim: Uses a counterfactual reviewer test to judge results: would the work be accepted even if done worse, which rewards honest negative results and controlled comparisons over bundled gains.
items.quote: Reviewers can set better incentives by asking: “Might I have accepted this paper if the authors had done a worse job?”

items.claim: Tests whether an explanation is real by asking if one would rely on it to make predictions or get a system working, separating genuine insight from decoration.
items.quote: Would I rely on this explanation for making predictions or for getting a system to work? This can be a good test of whether a theorem is being included to please reviewers or to convey actual insight.

items.claim: Values robustness checks across hyper-parameters and datasets over single-configuration results because gains may stem from tuning or dataset quirks rather than the claimed mechanism.
items.quote: Three practices that are common in the strongest empirical papers are error analysis, ablation studies, and robustness checks (to e.g. choice of hyper-parameters, as well as ideally to choice of dataset).

items.claim: Treats surprising apparent progress with suspicion, checking whether fair baselines with equal tuning erase the gain.
items.quote: Melis et al. [54] demonstrated that a series of published improvements, originally attributed to complex innovations in network architectures, were actually due to better hyper-parameter tuning. On equal footing, vanilla LSTMs, hardly modified since 1997 [32], topped the leaderboard.

items.claim: Holds standards as strong heuristics rather than unbreakable rules, accepting that important or costly results may justify skipping them.
items.quote: we present these as strong heuristics rather than unbreakable rules—if an idea cannot be shared without violating these heuristics, we prefer the idea be shared and the heuristics set aside.
